steps.step_body: Welcome to your first course project! Over the coming weeks, you will build a professional AP World History Writing Portfolio. This portfolio will include a full Document-Based Question (DBQ) response, a Long Essay Question (LEQ) response, and two high-level analytical outlines. By the end, you’ll have a tangible record of your mastery over the historical thinking skills needed for the AP exam. We are starting with the most critical skill: Document Analysis. In our recent sessions, we explored how cultural diffusion, technology, and environmental factors linked the world from 1200–1450. Today, you will select four primary sources related to these themes and begin a deep-dive analysis using the HIPP method (Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, and Point of View).

metadata.response_instruction: State your chosen theme and list the four primary sources you will analyze. Good work identifies sources that clearly relate to a single historical theme from the 1200-1450 period.

steps.step_body: To build a strong DBQ later, you need a cohesive set of documents. Choose a theme from our recent lessons: either 'Regional State-Building' (e.g., Song Dynasty bureaucracy or the Abbasid Caliphate) or 'Networks of Exchange' (e.g., Silk Road syncretism or the spread of Champa rice). Find four primary source snippets—these could be travelogues like Ibn Battuta, imperial edicts from the Song, or religious texts showing syncretism. Which theme have you chosen, and what are the titles or brief descriptions of your four selected sources?

metadata.response_instruction: Submit the Historical Context and Intended Audience analysis for your first two documents. High-quality responses connect the document to specific session concepts like Neo-Confucianism or Dar al-Islam.

steps.step_body: Now, let's start the HIPP analysis for your documents. For the first two documents, focus on the 'H' and 'I'. For Historical Context, don't just give a date; describe the broader trends (like the Song economic revolution or the rise of Sufism) that make the document meaningful. For Intended Audience, identify who the author was specifically trying to reach and how that influenced their tone. Draft these two components for your first two sources.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit the Purpose and Point of View (POV) analysis for your third and fourth documents. Ensure your POV analysis explains *why* the author's background matters to the document's reliability or perspective.

steps.step_body: For your remaining two documents, we will focus on Purpose and Point of View (POV). Purpose asks: why was this written? Was it to justify power, like a Neo-Confucian text, or to record observations, like a merchant's diary? For POV, consider the author's social status, religion, or occupation. How does being a scholar-gentry official or a Sufi missionary change the way they describe an event? Complete these analyses now.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your completed HIPP Document Sourcing Matrix as a PDF. It should include the source name and a detailed HIPP analysis for 4 sources. Criteria: accuracy of historical context, depth of sourcing analysis, and relevance to the 1200-1450 period.

steps.step_body: It's time to consolidate your work into the final deliverable for this stage: the HIPP Document Sourcing Matrix. Combine your findings into a single structured document or table. Each of the four sources must have at least one of the HIPP elements fully developed (though elite students often do more). This matrix will be your 'cheat sheet' when we move on to drafting your DBQ thesis and body paragraphs in the next stage.

Great job completing your first project milestone! As a final reflection, look at your four sources. How do they collectively show the 'Consequences of Connectivity' we discussed in class? Whether it's the spread of technology or the blending of religions, how does seeing these documents side-by-side change your understanding of the period? No formal submission is required here, but keep this connection in mind as we prepare to write your full essay.

stages.stage_title: DBQ Document Analysis and Sourcing Guide
stages.stage_description: Select a primary source set related to regional state-building or networks of exchange. Draft a sourcing analysis worksheet identifying historical context, audience, purpose, and point of view (HIPP analysis) for at least four documents to prepare for the DBQ.
stages.deliverable_increment: A completed HIPP Document Sourcing Matrix containing detailed analyses of 4 selected primary sources from the c. 1200-1450 period.

steps.step_body: In the previous stage, you meticulously analyzed primary sources from 1200–1450, focusing on the HIPP (Historical Situation, Intended Audience, Purpose, Point of View) method. You also recently explored how 'Gunpowder Empires' like the Ottomans, Mughals, and Qing used military technology and bureaucratic innovations to centralize power. Now, you will synthesize these skills to draft a full DBQ essay. This stage moves your portfolio from individual document analysis to a cohesive historical argument regarding imperial consolidation and global connectivity between 1450 and 1750.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a short list of 2-3 categories of evidence (e.g., 'Military Technology' or 'Bureaucratic Recruitment') that you will use as the basis for your body paragraphs. Good work identifies themes that can be supported by multiple documents.

steps.step_body: Your prompt for this DBQ is: 'Evaluate the extent to which land-based and maritime empires between 1450 and 1750 utilized similar methods to consolidate and maintain power.' To start, review the provided document set (found in your course resources) covering the Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals, and European maritime powers. Look for themes we discussed in lecture: gunpowder technology, elite bureaucracies (like the devshirme or zamindars), and religious legitimacy (like the Safavid use of Shi'ism). Briefly identify two or three 'buckets' or categories of evidence you will use to organize your essay.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your introductory paragraph. It will be evaluated on whether the contextualization is specific and relevant, and whether the thesis makes a clear, argumentative claim that addresses all parts of the prompt.

steps.step_body: Now, draft your introductory paragraph. It must include: 1) Contextualization: Describe the broader historical processes occurring at the time, such as the decline of feudalism or the rise of global trade networks (aim for 3-5 sentences). 2) A Thesis Statement: This must be a defensible claim that establishes a clear relationship between the methods of different empires. Avoid just listing; instead, use a 'complex' structure (e.g., 'While both land and maritime empires used X to consolidate power, they differed significantly in their use of Y because...').

It's time to build the core of your essay. For each body paragraph, you must: 1) State a topic sentence tied to your thesis. 2) Integrate evidence from at least seven documents (across the whole essay). 3) For at least four documents, explain HOW or WHY the document's HIPP (context, audience, purpose, or POV) is relevant to your argument. 4) Bring in 'Evidence Beyond the Documents'—specific historical facts not mentioned in the sources, such as the 'trace italienne' fortifications or the specific role of the Janissaries.

To earn the 'Complexity' point on the AP rubric, you need to demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of the historical process. You can do this by explaining both similarities and differences, or by showing how a single development had multiple, contradictory effects (e.g., how the zamindar system both funded the Mughal state and eventually led to its decentralization). Review your draft and ensure you haven't just described documents, but have used them to support a nuanced argument about imperial power.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your full DBQ essay as a PDF. Good work includes a complex thesis, specific contextualization, use of all/most documents to support an argument, at least four instances of sourcing (HIPP) analysis, and at least one piece of outside evidence.

steps.step_body: You have reached the culmination of this stage. Review your work one last time to ensure it is approximately 800-1000 words, follows a logical structure, and explicitly addresses the prompt. Check that your HIPP analysis is woven into the narrative rather than added as a list at the end. Once satisfied, submit your complete essay for the portfolio.

stages.stage_title: DBQ Essay Drafting: Land and Maritime Empires
stages.stage_description: Synthesize the historical documents analyzed in the previous stage with your knowledge of imperial administration and global exchange. Write a fully developed Document-Based Essay that features a complex thesis statement, contextualization, and integrated document evidence.
stages.deliverable_increment: A complete, typed DBQ Essay (approx. 800-1000 words) addressing a prompt on imperial consolidation and connectivity from 1450 to 1750.

steps.step_body: In our previous stages, you analyzed primary sources from the medieval era and drafted a DBQ on the consolidation of land and maritime empires (1450–1750). We are now moving into the modern era (Units 3 and 4). Building on our recent lectures regarding the collapse of land-based empires like the Qing and Ottomans, the structural causes of WWI (MAIN), and the horrific rise of state-sponsored mass violence, this stage tasks you with writing a comparative Long Essay Question (LEQ). This will be a key component of your final portfolio, demonstrating your ability to synthesize historical reasoning across different global contexts.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your chosen prompt number and the two specific historical cases you will compare. Good work identifies cases with enough 'connective tissue' for a high-level comparison.

steps.step_body: To begin your LEQ, you must choose a focus that allows for a deep comparison between Unit 3 (Revolutions/Industrialization) and Unit 4 (Global Conflict). Choose one of the following prompts: 1) Compare the causes of the collapse of two land-based empires (Ottoman, Russian, or Qing) between 1900 and 1920. 2) Compare the extent to which state-sponsored mass violence was driven by ideology versus wartime crisis in two different 20th-century contexts (e.g., the Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide). 3) Compare the roles of nationalism and militarism in triggering global conflict in the early 20th century. Which prompt have you chosen, and which two historical examples will you use as your basis for comparison?

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your introductory paragraph. It should provide broad background information that is relevant to the prompt but does not yet state your specific thesis.

steps.step_body: An AP-aligned LEQ must begin with contextualization. Before you dive into your specific comparison, you need to set the stage. Think about the global trends occurring during the period of your prompt. For example, if you are discussing imperial collapse, mention the broader shift from traditional autocracies to industrial nation-states and the pressures of global imperialism. Draft a 3-5 sentence introduction that places your topic within the broader 'flow' of world history.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your thesis statement. It must be a historically defensible claim that establishes a clear roadmap for your essay's argument.

steps.step_body: Now, draft your thesis statement. A high-scoring LEQ thesis does more than just restate the prompt; it must make a defensible claim that addresses both similarities and differences (or multiple causes/effects). Use the 'Although [Counter-argument], because [Evidence A] and [Evidence B], [Main Argument]' formula. For instance: 'Although both the Ottoman and Russian empires collapsed due to internal ethnic nationalism, the Russian collapse was more significantly accelerated by the industrial grievances of an urban working class, whereas the Ottoman collapse was driven by the failure of secularizing reforms.'

It is time to write the core of your essay (approx. 400-600 words). Focus on using specific historical evidence to support your thesis. If you are comparing the Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide, you should discuss specific administrative systems, racial pseudo-science, or the 'cover' provided by WWI and WWII. Ensure you use transition words that signal comparison (e.g., 'similarly,' 'conversely,' 'in contrast to'). Your goal is to move beyond just listing facts about two events and instead explain *why* they are similar or different based on the historical reasoning of causation or comparison.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your completed LEQ essay as a PDF. Good work features a clear thesis, at least 3-4 pieces of specific historical evidence, and a sustained argument that connects back to the prompt throughout the response.

steps.step_body: Assemble your introduction, thesis, and body paragraphs into a final draft of 600-800 words. Review your work against the AP LEQ rubric: Do you have a clear thesis? Have you provided at least two specific pieces of evidence for each side of your comparison? Did you use historical reasoning to explain the relationship between your examples? Once you've polished the draft, submit it here.

stages.stage_title: LEQ Drafting: Comparing Global Transformations and Conflicts
stages.stage_description: Construct a complete Long Essay Question (LEQ) response comparing either the causes of industrialization, imperial expansions, or the geopolitical crises of global conflicts. Focus heavily on historical reasoning (causation or comparison) and providing specific historical evidence.
stages.deliverable_increment: A fully drafted LEQ Essay (approx. 600-800 words) answering a comparative prompt spanning Unit 3 (Revolutions/Industrialization) and Unit 4 (Global Conflict).

steps.step_body: You have already mastered the art of sourcing documents and drafting full comparative essays on land and maritime empires. Now, we shift our focus to the mid-to-late 20th century. Having just explored the collapse of the Soviet Union and the rise of grassroots resistance movements like Solidarity, you are ready to analyze how these global shifts intersected with decolonization. In this stage, you will plan an argumentation structure that tackles the dual pressures of superpower rivalry and the quest for national sovereignty.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your drafted thesis statement. A successful response will include a clear claim, a specific line of reasoning (the 'because' part), and an acknowledgment of multiple perspectives or historical nuances.

steps.step_body: Start by drafting a thesis statement for the following prompt: 'To what extent did the Cold War facilitate or hinder the decolonization process in the period 1945–1990?' A strong AP-style thesis must do more than restate the prompt; it needs to establish a clear line of reasoning and acknowledge complexity. Try to incorporate a 'counter-argument' starter (like 'While...' or 'Despite...') to set yourself up for the complexity point later. For example, consider how superpowers provided aid to some movements but suppressed others to maintain their 'spheres of influence.'

Now that you have your thesis, outline three main arguments to support it. One paragraph should focus on how Cold War aid (military or economic) accelerated independence. A second should examine how proxy wars or 'containment' hindered sovereignty. A third should address the Non-Aligned Movement as an attempt to find a 'third way' between the US and USSR. For each, write a clear topic sentence that links directly back to your thesis.

An outline is only as good as its evidence. For each of your three planned paragraphs, list at least two specific historical examples. Think back to our sessions: the Aswan High Dam in Egypt, the Vietnam War, the Truman Doctrine, or the Bandung Conference. Don't just name them; briefly note how they prove your specific point about decolonization.

metadata.response_instruction: Provide a brief paragraph (3-4 sentences) explaining which complexity strategy you will use (e.g., counter-argument, change over time, or multiple perspectives) and how it challenges or deepens your main thesis.

steps.step_body: To earn the AP Complexity point, you must show you understand that history isn't one-sided. In your outline, identify where you will address a counter-argument or a significant shift over time. For instance, you might explain how a movement started as a purely nationalist struggle but was forced to adopt a communist or capitalist ideology to survive in the bipolar world order. Briefly explain why you chose this specific point of complexity.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your final Decolonization Argumentation Plan in PDF format. The document must include: a complex thesis, three body paragraph outlines (topic sentence + 2 pieces of evidence each), and a dedicated section for your complexity argument.

steps.step_body: It is time to assemble your work into a formal plan. Combine your thesis, your three topic sentences with their associated evidence lists, and your complexity plan into one cohesive document. This outline serves as the structural backbone for the final analytical piece of your portfolio.

stages.stage_description: Formulate a strong, arguable thesis and a detailed paragraph outline addressing the Cold War's impact on decolonization movements. Incorporate counter-arguments to demonstrate the complexity required for the AP complexity point.
stages.deliverable_increment: A formal LEQ/DBQ outline with a complex thesis statement, topic sentences, and specific evidence lists for the Cold War and Decolonization era.

steps.step_body: Welcome to the final stage of your AP World History Writing Portfolio! Over the past units, you have analyzed early modern sources, drafted a DBQ on land and maritime empires, and written a comparative LEQ on industrial transformations and global conflicts. In the previous session, we explored the 'Great Acceleration'—how post-1945 technological leaps, the Green Revolution, and medical breakthroughs like vaccines reshaped human life. Now, you will bring these threads together. This final stage asks you to look at the contemporary era (1900–present) to see how globalization creates both deep continuity with the past and radical changes in how we live, eat, and relate to one another.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your complex thesis statement. A strong response will include both a continuity and a change, using specific historical terminology (e.g., glocalization, digital infrastructure, or national sovereignty).

steps.step_body: To begin your final outline, you need a complex thesis statement that addresses the prompt: 'Evaluate the extent to which globalized commerce and communication changed cultural identities and economic systems from 1900 to the present.' Your thesis must identify at least one continuity (something that stayed the same, like the persistence of local traditions or nationalism) and one change (such as 'cultural hybridization' or the shift to a digital service economy). Aim for a 'Despite X, Y and Z' structure to show complexity.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a structured outline for a 3-paragraph essay. For each paragraph, provide a topic sentence and at least two specific pieces of evidence (e.g., 'Green Revolution HYVs' or 'Global sports events').

steps.step_body: Now, build the skeleton of your globalization outline. You need to organize your evidence into three body paragraphs. Focus on the vectors we discussed: Migration, Communication, and Commerce. For example, you might use the Green Revolution as evidence of economic change or 'cultural hybridization' (like the McAloo Tikki) as evidence of cultural adaptation. Ensure you also include evidence of resistance to globalization, such as movements to preserve indigenous languages or protect national industries from multinational corporations. This ensures your argument is balanced and meets the AP requirement for 'multiple perspectives.'

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your 300-word meta-reflective introduction. Good work will connect specific skills (e.g., HIPP analysis) to the broader themes of the course (e.g., connectivity and power).

steps.step_body: To tie your entire portfolio together (from the 1200s to today), write a 300-word meta-reflective introduction. This is not just an intro to your globalization outline; it is a reflection on your journey through this course. Explain how the historical thinking skills you’ve practiced—like contextualization and sourcing—helped you understand the transition from early maritime empires to the hyper-connected digital world of today. How does seeing the 'long view' of history change your perspective on current global issues like climate change or consumerism?

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your final document containing the Structured Analytical Outline and the 300-word Meta-Reflective Introduction. Your submission will be evaluated on the complexity of the thesis and the depth of the reflection connecting the current unit to previous course themes.

steps.step_body: It is time to finalize your deliverable. Take your globalization outline and your meta-reflection from the previous steps and combine them into a single document. This document represents the fourth and final component of your portfolio, following your DBQ, sourcing matrix, and LEQ. Review your work one last time to ensure you have used the historical terms from Unit 6, such as 'time-space compression' or 'technological acceleration,' to demonstrate mastery of the contemporary era content.

Congratulations! You have completed a full AP World History Writing Portfolio. By tracing global dynamics from the post-classical era to the digital age, you have built the exact skills needed for the AP exam. You can now see how the movements of the 13th-century Silk Road paved the way for the 21st-century internet. Keep this portfolio as a reference for your exam review—it contains your strongest arguments and evidence sets.

stages.stage_description: Create a final analytical essay outline assessing continuity and change in global economics and culture during the contemporary era (1900 to present), tying together all portfolio components with a meta-reflective introduction.
stages.deliverable_increment: A structured analytical outline for contemporary globalization, combined with a 300-word introductory meta-reflection to complete the final 4-part portfolio.

projects.project_name: AP World History DBQ and LEQ Portfolio: Tracing the Dynamics of Global History (1200–Present)
projects.final_deliverable: A comprehensive 4-part AP World History Writing Portfolio consisting of one fully drafted DBQ response with a detailed sourcing table (focused on Unit 1-2 connections), one fully drafted Comparative LEQ response (focused on Unit 3-4 transformations), and two analytical outlines (for Units 5 and 6) showing mastered AP World History argumentation.
projects.project_description: Throughout this course, you will construct a comprehensive, AP-aligned DBQ (Document-Based Question) and LEQ (Long Essay Question) portfolio. You will apply core historical thinking skills—such as contextualization, thesis construction, sourcing analysis, and causal argumentation—to compile a structured AP history writing portfolio that targets the exact rubrics used on the AP World History: Modern exam.
